title: Judges 7:1–8
context: Judges 6 introduced Gideon, called by the LORD to save Israel from seven years of Midianite oppression (6:1, 14). He tore down his father’s altar to Baal, earning the name Jerubbaal (6:32), and the LORD’s Spirit came on him to rally the tribes (6:34). After the signs of the fleece (6:36–40), Judges 7:1–8 shows the LORD reducing Gideon’s army from thousands to three hundred. The stated reason is given in 7:2: so that Israel would not boast, “My own hand has saved me.” The section teaches, in both traditions’ reading, that deliverance belongs to the LORD and that he is free to save by few as well as by many.

verses.text: Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, and all the people who were with him, rose up early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. Midian’s camp was on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator gives both of Gideon’s names, “Jerubbaal, who is Gideon,” recalling his stand against Baal in 6:25–32. The armies face each other near the spring of Harod and the hill of Moreh. Arminian readers note that Gideon rises early and takes up his position, responding in obedience to a call he had once doubted (6:15), and that his earlier hesitancy did not disqualify him from God’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the scene is set by God’s prior call and the coming of his Spirit on Gideon (6:34). The man who called himself “the least in my father’s house” (6:15) now leads Israel because the LORD has chosen and equipped him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of a deliverance that God initiates and Gideon carries out, setting the stage for the reduction of the army.

verses.text: The LORD said to Gideon, “The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the people are “too many,” lest Israel boast, “My own hand has saved me.” Arminian readers note God’s concern for the hearts of his people. He shapes the circumstances to guard them against pride and to draw them into grateful trust, echoing the warning of Deuteronomy 8:17 against saying “My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers highlight the purpose clause: God arranges the victory so that the glory is unmistakably his. Paul states the same principle when he says God chose the weak things “that no flesh should boast before God” (1 Corinthians 1:29). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as teaching that salvation belongs to the LORD and that human boasting has no place before him.

verses.text: Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return and depart from Mount Gilead.’ ” So twenty-two thousand of the people returned, and ten thousand remained.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who are “fearful and trembling” may go home, following the principle of Deuteronomy 20:8, where the fearful are sent back “lest his brother’s heart melt as his heart.” Twenty-two thousand leave. Arminian readers note that the choice is left to each man, and many take it. The mention of Mount Gilead here is puzzling geographically, and interpreters explain it in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD himself thinning the ranks through his appointed means, as the law had already provided for the fearful. The departure of two thirds of the army sets up a victory no one could credit to numbers. Shared ground: both traditions read the release of the fearful as an act of mercy within Israel’s law and as the first step in showing that the battle is the LORD’s.

verses.text: The LORD said to Gideon, “There are still too many people. Bring them down to the water, and I will test them for you there. It shall be, that those whom I tell you, ‘This shall go with you,’ shall go with you; and whoever I tell you, ‘This shall not go with you,’ shall not go.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ten thousand are “still too many,” and the LORD says he will “test them for you there.” Arminian readers note that God involves Gideon at each step, telling him plainly who goes and who stays. The process builds Gideon’s trust as he watches his army shrink in obedience to God’s word rather than by his own judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the LORD alone determines who goes: “those whom I tell you … shall go with you.” The selection rests entirely on his word. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God choosing the instruments of his deliverance, and neither tradition turns the episode into a statement about individual salvation; it concerns the means of a particular victory.

verses.text: So he brought down the people to the water; and the LORD said to Gideon, “Everyone who laps of the water with his tongue, like a dog laps, you shall set him by himself; likewise everyone who bows down on his knees to drink.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon brings the people to the water, and the LORD separates those who lap “like a dog laps” from those who kneel to drink. Arminian readers note that the text does not say the test measured alertness or courage. Interpreters differ on whether the method was meaningful in itself or simply the means God chose to reach a small number.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the narrative stresses the LORD’s instruction rather than any merit in the drinking method. The selection serves God’s purpose of reducing the army, not of rewarding the best soldiers. Shared ground: both traditions caution against reading too much into the detail, and both see its point in the outcome: a tiny force through which God will act.

verses.text: The number of those who lapped, putting their hand to their mouth, was three hundred men; but all the rest of the people bowed down on their knees to drink water.
verses.arminianNotes: Three hundred men lap “putting their hand to their mouth,” while all the rest kneel. The verse’s description is not fully clear, and interpreters picture the action differently. Arminian readers note that the result leaves Gideon with a force of about one percent of his starting army, a stark test of his willingness to trust God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the small number a vivid demonstration that God does not depend on human strength. Jonathan later states the principle: “there is no restraint on the LORD to save by many or by few” (1 Samuel 14:6). Shared ground: both traditions read the three hundred as a sign that the coming victory will be clearly the LORD’s work.

verses.text: The LORD said to Gideon, “I will save you by the three hundred men who lapped, and deliver the Midianites into your hand. Let all the other people go, each to his own place.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises, “I will save you by the three hundred men who lapped.” Arminian readers note that the promise calls Gideon to act in faith on God’s word, sending the rest home before seeing any result. God’s promise and Gideon’s obedience go together, and the obedience is costly when the enemy is so numerous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers highlight that the LORD is the subject of the verb: “I will save you.” The three hundred are his instrument, not the source of victory. Shared ground: God’s promise to save “by the three hundred” is common ground for both traditions, teaching that salvation belongs to the LORD and that he delights to work through weakness (compare 2 Corinthians 4:7).

verses.text: So the people took food in their hand, and their trumpets; and he sent all the rest of the men of Israel to their own tents, but retained the three hundred men; and the camp of Midian was beneath him in the valley.
verses.arminianNotes: The three hundred keep the provisions and trumpets of the departing men, and the camp of Midian lies “beneath him in the valley.” Arminian readers note the tension of the moment: a small band now faces a vast army, and Gideon must continue trusting God’s word as the odds grow visibly against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the practical detail of the trumpets, which will become the means of victory in 7:16–22. God has already provided what is needed, though Gideon does not yet know how it will be used. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a transition that heightens the drama and shows God preparing the outcome in ways not yet visible.
